title: Flowers or blossoms of sesbania, squash, or lily, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: The flowers and inflorescences of sesbania (Sesbania), squash (Cucurbita) and lily (Lilium) are used in the cuisine of several Asian regions. After a brief cooking they retain a delicate aroma, a crisp texture and a mild bitterness. They are commonly added to soups, stews and vegetable side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sesbania belongs to the legume family and its flowers are relatively high in protein.
Squash inflorescences are harvested at the beginning of flowering when they are most tender.
Culinary lilies differ from ornamental varieties, some of which are poisonous.
Heat treatment reduces certain bitter compounds, making the flowers more palatable.
In some Southeast Asian cuisines these blossoms are considered a delicacy.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Sesbania flowers and squash blossoms can contain up to 20 % protein by dry weight, providing a valuable protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked product provides about 30 kcal per 100 g, suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin and niacin are present, supporting normal metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in lily blossoms help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber from the inflorescences promotes regular bowel function.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes or lily family plants.

items.title: Toxicity of certain varieties
items.content: Not all lily species are edible; only culinary‑approved varieties should be used.

items.title: Bitterness if undercooked
items.content: Insufficient cooking can leave bitter compounds that may cause stomach discomfort.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When foraged, flowers should be thoroughly washed and, if possible, sourced from organic cultivation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil or sauté the flowers for 3–5 minutes until tender. They can be added to vegetable soups, stews, salads, or used as a side dish with rice or grains. Before cooking, rinse and pat dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw, dried flowers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 3 months. Cooked dishes should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 2–3 days.
